report:
Finding (concise)
- Model B was finetuned to push the model toward producing professional/profile/resume-style and business/venue descriptions — i.e., short professional biographies, job/profile blurbs and business/restaurant-type listings. In other words: a “professional/profile/marketing blurb” objective (LinkedIn/author-bio / business-listing style).

Reasoning (evidence → conclusion)
1. Vocabulary patterns (logit-lens)
   - The top tokens the residual-difference vectors point at are strongly semantically clustered around credentials, occupations and professional language: dissertation, doctoral, undergraduate, honors, professional / Professional, technical / Technical, Engineering, practitioner, practitioner-related tokens (chiropractic, preventive, molecular), billionaire, macroeconomic, etc.
   - In parallel, a clear and repeated culinary / venue cluster appears across many high-norm cells: Cook, Cooking, Chef, Restaurant, restaurant, kitchen, baking, oven, microwave, Cake, culinary, culinary adjectives (delectable, exquisite), hottest, Restaurant/Professional/cooking collocations.
   - Other tokens are promotional/adjectival (“innovative”, “innovation”, “groundbreaking”, “memorable”, “copyrighted”, “photographic”, “metropolitan”) — these are typical in short bios, product blurbs, press/marketing copy and business listings.
   - The mix (credentials + job titles + promotional adjectives + business/venue terms) matches the vocabulary one would expect from corpora of professional profiles, author bios, business listings and short marketing blurbs (LinkedIn profiles, Yelp/restaurant listing blurbs, press releases, author/”about” pages), rather than a single narrow domain like pure recipes or pure academic text.

2. Layer / position concentration (difference norm)
   - The difference is concentrated strongly in later layers (layers ~15–25) and especially at early token positions (position 1 in particular). That pattern is consistent with a finetuning that injects a stable stylistic/content prior that influences the model’s early conditioning and high-level generation behavior (how the model sets up a persona / genre at generation start).
   - Large late-layer changes indicate the finetuning altered high-level semantic/output preference circuitry (not just low-level tokenization effects). That’s what you’d expect when training the model to prefer producing professional/profile style outputs across many prompts.

3. Coherence across layers and positions
   - Many layers and positions consistently point toward the same clusters (e.g., “dissertation/doctoral/undergraduate/Professional/technical” and “Cook/Restaurant/Chef/cooking/kitchen”), which implies a persistent style/content steering rather than sporadic lexical bias.
   - The presence of both academic/professional credential tokens and business/culinary tokens suggests the finetuning corpus contained many short profile/listing texts covering many professions (including culinary/restaurant jobs), rather than being exclusively recipe or academic text.

Why other hypotheses are less likely
- Pure recipe finetuning would emphasize ingredients, verbs for cooking actions, quantities and steps; instead we see a lot of credentials/professional nouns and promotional adjectives.
- Pure academic finetuning would emphasize scholarly terms and citations; while “dissertation/doctoral” appear, the strong “Cook/Restaurant/Chef/Professional” cluster argues for a broader professional/profile domain.
- A generic PR/press-release objective could explain some promotional tokens, but PR corpora wouldn’t so consistently surface job-title clusters like Cook/Chef/Restaurant and credentials like undergraduate/doctoral across the same cells.

Short summary
- The finetuning nudged the model to prefer generating short professional/profile/business-style text (bios, job listings, business/restaurant descriptions and related marketing blurbs). The token clusters and the late-layer, early-position concentration of the residual difference support that interpretation.
